base_ingredients.name: Dried chickpeas
base_ingredients.note: Soak for 12–24 h in cold water. Do NOT cook: falafel uses soaked chickpeas only — cooked chickpeas produce a paste-like mixture that will not hold its shape. Not to be confused with ta'amia (Egyptian falafel made from fava beans) — that is a different dish.

matrix.consequence: No sweet backbone: the dish tastes one-dimensional, the chickpeas dominate without aromatic support.
A barely perceptible hint of sweetness — noticeably mild to most palates. Texture of the raw mixture is actually better, though: less moisture.
Effectively the same result as 1× for most people: slightly less sweet, but within the tolerance zone.
Correct sweetness and aromatic depth; the onion's moisture contribution is accounted for in the recipe.
The onion releases extra liquid: the mixture becomes wetter, more binder is needed, the result is denser.
Clear excess moisture in the raw mixture — significantly more flour is required to compensate. Onion flavour starts to dominate.

variants.title: Fresh
variants.detail: Standard. Releases moisture when cut or processed — factor this into binding the mixture.

variants.title: Onion powder
variants.detail: ~1 tsp instead of 80 g. No moisture contribution — the mixture will be drier and may need little or no binder. Flavour is more concentrated and uniform.

variants.title: Shallot
variants.detail: More delicate, slightly sweeter, less moisture. Same quantity or 10% more.

variants.title: Scallion
variants.detail: Milder, less sweet. White and light-green parts only, ~60 g instead of 80 g.

variants.title: Red onion
variants.detail: Sharper raw flavour, more colour. Same quantity.

substitutions.title: Shallot
substitutions.detail: Closest substitute, slightly more refined flavour.

substitutions.title: Onion powder
substitutions.detail: Works if reducing the mixture's moisture is acceptable.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: Viable in falafel — the dish still works, just with less sweet depth.

matrix.consequence: Flavour is softer and more neutral; the spices taste less amplified.
A faint background note — most people will not tell it apart from none at all.
Noticeable but subtle; the spices come through cleanly without competition. Barely distinguishable from 1×.
A clear garlic note without dominating; amplifies cumin and coriander effectively.
Garlic becomes noticeable as its own flavour and starts to compete with the spices. After cooking it is milder than raw.
Garlic dominates. In the raw mixture the sharpness is aggressive; cooking softens it, but the imbalance with the spices remains.

variants.title: Fresh cloves
variants.detail: Standard. Sharpest, most complex flavour.

variants.title: Garlic powder
variants.detail: ½ tsp instead of 3 cloves. No moisture, evenly distributed, milder and more uniform flavour — but it lacks fresh garlic's volatile bite.

variants.title: Roasted garlic
variants.detail: Much sweeter and milder. 5–6 roasted cloves instead of 3 raw. Changes the character significantly: less pungent, more sweet.

variants.title: Garlic oil
variants.detail: Gives flavour without texture — not suitable for the falafel mixture.

substitutions.title: Garlic powder (reduced quantity)
substitutions.detail: Acceptable workaround.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: Acceptable. Flavour becomes milder.

substitutions.title: No direct substitute
substitutions.detail: Nothing replicates fresh garlic's specific volatile compounds.

matrix.consequence: The interior is beige-brown, the flavour earthier and heavier. The dish is still fully functional — omission is acceptable.
A faint herbal note; colour barely visible on the cross-section.
Visible green flecks; flavour present but not assertive. Within the tolerance zone for most recipes.
Clear green flecks on the cross-section, a fresh contrast to the earthy chickpeas. Herb flavour noticeable but balanced.
The herb flavour starts to compete with the spices; the mixture is slightly wetter.
Herbal taste overpowers the spices. The mixture is noticeably wetter — additional binder may be required. The interior becomes very green.

variants.title: Fresh
variants.detail: Standard. Contributes moisture and bright colour. Refrigerate and use within 3 days of purchase for best colour retention.

variants.title: Dried
variants.detail: ~1½ tsp instead of 25 g (ratio ~1:4 by volume). No moisture contribution, no green colour on the cross-section; flavour is more concentrated but less fresh. Acceptable in a pinch — noticeably different.

variants.title: Frozen
variants.detail: Behaves like fresh once thawed but releases more water — blot thoroughly dry before use.

substitutions.title: Cilantro
substitutions.detail: Same quantity. Traditional in Levantine-style falafel. More citrusy and assertive — a divisive flavour, but authentic.

substitutions.title: Dill
substitutions.detail: ~15 g instead of 25 g. Significantly different profile (more Eastern European character), not traditional in falafel.

substitutions.title: Basil
substitutions.detail: NOT recommended — clashes with cumin and coriander.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: Fully acceptable. The dish works without herbs.

matrix.consequence: Falafel loses its identity: it tastes like seasoned chickpeas, not falafel. Structurally fine, but culturally unrecognisable.
A faint cumin note lacking depth. An option for those who dislike assertive spices.
Recognisable but restrained; coriander comes forward. Acceptable for sensitive palates.
Correct Levantine profile. Works in balance with the coriander — neither dominates.
Cumin begins to tip toward bitterness, especially at air fryer temperatures. The balance with the coriander shifts.
A clear bitter note; cumin overpowers the coriander. The dish becomes unpleasantly astringent.

variants.title: Pre-ground from a packet
variants.detail: Standard. Loses potency about 6 months after opening — sniff the packet: if the aroma is faint, use more.

variants.title: Freshly ground from toasted seeds
variants.detail: Noticeably more aromatic. Method: dry-toast whole seeds in a pan for 1–2 min until they begin to pop and smell fragrant, cool completely, grind in the Cecotec chopper or a mortar. Preferred grind for falafel: medium — not powder. Small spice fragments add character and texture.

variants.title: Whole seeds in the mixture
variants.detail: NOT recommended: cumin seeds are small and hard — they create unpleasant sharp fragments.

substitutions.title: Caraway
substitutions.detail: The closest botanical relative. Use ¾ the quantity. Slightly different profile — more European, less Middle Eastern. Not traditional but functional.

substitutions.title: Nothing else substitutes well
substitutions.detail: Cumin's specific volatile compounds (cuminaldehyde) have no close analogue among common spices.

matrix.consequence: Without coriander, cumin becomes oppressively earthy. The flavour is one-dimensional and heavy.
Cumin outweighs the coriander. The citrusy note is present but insufficient to balance.
Noticeably more cumin-forward. Acceptable for those who prefer earthy over citrusy.
Earthy and citrusy in balance; the flavour is rounded and complex. Cumin and coriander are used in equal quantities precisely because they balance each other.
Coriander starts to dominate. The profile tips toward citrusy-floral and loses its Middle Eastern character.
The cumin is buried. The dish tastes like something from a different regional cuisine.

variants.title: Pre-ground from a packet
variants.detail: Same freshness caveat as cumin: after ~6 months the aroma fades.

variants.title: Freshly ground from toasted seeds
variants.detail: Same method as for cumin. Coriander seeds are softer and larger than cumin seeds — a slightly coarser grind is fine; medium-coarse is appropriate for falafel and adds texture.

variants.title: Whole seeds
variants.detail: Possible as an intentional textural element: coriander seeds are softer than cumin and will not create unpleasant fragments. Not traditional, but edible — only if intentional.

substitutions.title: Fresh coriander leaf (cilantro)
substitutions.detail: NOT a drop-in replacement for the seed: the leaf and the seed have related but distinct flavour compounds.

substitutions.title: Ground cardamom
substitutions.detail: ~¼ tsp can add a citrusy-floral note, but changes the flavour direction noticeably.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: Better than a poor substitute: if coriander is unavailable, simply reduce the cumin proportionally.

matrix.consequence: All flavours — spices, herbs, garlic — are noticeably muted. The dish tastes flat and dull; everyone notices.
Flavour is present but restrained; the spices don't fully express. Most people notice.
Perceptibly underseasoned to an attentive palate. Acceptable to those who restrict salt.
Salt enhances without tasting salty. All other flavours come forward fully.
Saltiness is perceptible as its own note; the spices taste sharper. Noticeable to most people.
Salt dominates, the spices are overwhelmed. The dish is unpleasant.

variants.title: Fine sea or table salt
variants.detail: Standard for falafel: dissolves evenly in the mixture.

variants.title: Coarse salt
variants.detail: Dissolves unevenly in a raw mixture — not recommended unless ground first.

variants.title: Fleur de sel / salt flakes
variants.detail: Finishing salt only, not for mixing into the raw mixture.

substitutions.title: None
substitutions.detail: Nothing preserves salt's flavour-amplification function. Reduce only for dietary reasons, knowing the flavour impact.

substitutions.title: Soy sauce
substitutions.detail: Not appropriate: introduces liquid and umami — not for the falafel mixture.

matrix.consequence: Almost unnoticeable in a spiced mixture. A slightly simpler finish.
Barely perceptible warmth. Within the very wide tolerance zone.
Present but subtle. Within the broad tolerance zone.
Gentle warmth in the finish. Adds complexity without asserting itself.
Pepper is slightly more assertive, yet still pleasant for most.
Pepper is noticeable as its own flavour. Fine for pepper lovers; reduce if serving people who dislike heat.

variants.title: Pre-ground
variants.detail: Standard.

variants.title: Freshly ground
variants.detail: Slightly more aromatic — a minor improvement over pre-ground.

variants.title: White pepper
variants.detail: Milder, less aromatic, same quantity.

substitutions.title: White pepper
substitutions.detail: Same quantity, milder.

substitutions.title: Smoked paprika
substitutions.detail: Adds smokiness, not heat — changes the flavour direction rather than substituting.

substitutions.title: Cayenne pepper
substitutions.detail: Much hotter. Use ¼ the quantity.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: Barely noticeable in a mixture with cumin and coriander.

ingredients.name: Baking powder
ingredients.necessity_note: A Western adaptation for the air fryer, not tradition. In deep-frying, hot oil creates an explosive steam lift that aerates the interior by itself — an air fryer lacks this mechanism, and a small dose of baking powder partially compensates for the difference. Makes the texture slightly lighter; not obligatory.

matrix.consequence: A dense, heavy interior — fully authentic: this is exactly what traditional deep-fried falafel is like. Acceptable in the air fryer, but noticeably denser.
Marginal difference from the norm — the interior is only a little denser.
Within the tolerance zone for most people.
A slightly lighter, more open crumb. Partially compensates for the air fryer's lack of the deep-fry explosive steam lift.
Balls become fragile — they crack or break when turned or transferred.
Structural failure plus a metallic-soapy aftertaste from excess baking powder.

substitutions.title: Baking soda
substitutions.detail: ¼ the quantity (~¼ tsp instead of 1 tsp). Requires an acid to activate, and standard falafel has none — the soda will not fully activate and may leave a metallic note. Only if you also add lemon juice or yogurt.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: The traditional and correct choice.

ingredients.name: Flour
ingredients.necessity_note: A safety net for a wet mixture, not tradition. Needed only if: the chickpeas were not dried thoroughly, the onion released excess moisture, or the mixture was over-processed into a paste. With correct drying and correct pulsing, no flour is needed at all. The amount is determined by the ball test, not by a fixed number.

matrix.consequence: The mixture does not bind: balls fall apart immediately or disintegrate in the air fryer. Exception: with perfect technique, zero flour is the correct option.
Holds shape when cold, but cracks or crumbles when heated.
May be sufficient if the mixture is only slightly wet. Verify with the ball test.
"1×" means however much the ball test requires, not a fixed gram value. Correct cohesion: the ball holds its shape at room temperature and does not stick to the palm.
The interior is slightly denser and starts to taste floury.
A dense, doughy interior with a clear flour taste. The light, crumbly texture of good falafel is lost.

substitutions.title: Chickpea flour
substitutions.detail: Same role and quantity range; enhances flavour coherence (an all-chickpea dish). Slightly more hygroscopic — start with half the wheat flour amount and add gradually. Gluten-free.

substitutions.title: Cornstarch
substitutions.detail: ½ the quantity — binds tighter with less bulk. Neutral flavour, no colour impact.

substitutions.title: Omission
substitutions.detail: The correct answer if technique is right. Always try zero flour first and verify with the ball test.

steps.title: Soak the chickpeas
steps.what: Cover 250 g of dried chickpeas generously with cold water (about three times their volume) and leave for 12–24 h at room temperature. Do not cook them — falafel uses soaked chickpeas only.
steps.done_when: A chickpea breaks apart easily between your fingers and the centre is matte throughout — no dry, glassy core.
steps.if_skipped: Dry or under-soaked chickpeas will not grind into a couscous-like grain — the balls come out hard and stay raw inside.

steps.title: Drain and dry the chickpeas thoroughly
steps.what: Drain the chickpeas in a colander, spread them in a single layer on a towel and blot with a second towel on top; let them sit for 10–15 min. The drier the chickpeas, the lower the chance you will need flour.
steps.done_when: The surface of the chickpeas feels dry and loose, and the towel underneath no longer picks up wet marks.
steps.if_skipped: A wet mixture will not hold its shape — you will have to compensate with flour, and the texture becomes denser.

steps.title: Roughly chop the onion, garlic and parsley
steps.what: Peel the onion and garlic, strip the parsley leaves from the stems. Cut the onion into 6–8 pieces so the processor works evenly.

equipment.settings: knife and board; onion into 6–8 pieces

steps.done_when: Pieces are roughly the same size, ready for even processing.
steps.if_skipped: Large uneven chunks process unevenly: paste in some places, whole pieces of onion in others.

steps.title: Pulse everything in the Kenwood FDP22
steps.what: Load the chickpeas, onion, garlic, parsley, spices, salt and pepper into the Kenwood FDP22, filling no more than half of the 2.1 L bowl — work in two batches if needed. Grind in short 1–2 s pulses, scraping down the sides between rounds.

equipment.settings: fill ≤ ½ of the bowl; 1–2 s pulses

steps.done_when: The mixture looks like a moist grain (like couscous), not a paste: individual granules are visible to the eye.
steps.if_skipped: Running continuously instead of pulsing produces a hummus-like paste — the balls come out dense and will require flour.
steps.calibration: Consistency test: squeeze a handful of the mixture in your fist — it should clump and hold together. If it crumbles apart — 1–2 more pulses; if it smears like a paste — it is over-processed, rescue it with flour at step 6.

steps.title: Chill the mixture
steps.what: Cover the mixture with a lid or plastic wrap and refrigerate for 30–60 min. The cold firms up the mixture and makes shaping noticeably easier.

equipment.settings: +4 °C, covered with a lid or wrap

steps.done_when: The mixture is cold to the touch and noticeably firmer than before chilling.
steps.if_skipped: A warm mixture sticks to your hands, and the balls hold their shape poorly during shaping and turning.

steps.title: Ball test; flour if needed
steps.what: Form one test ball of ~30 g and squeeze it in your palm: it should hold its shape and not stick. If it falls apart, work in flour 1 tbsp at a time, repeating the test after each spoonful.

equipment.settings: flour 1 tbsp at a time, usually no more than 2

steps.done_when: The test ball holds its shape at room temperature and leaves no sticky residue on your palm.
steps.if_skipped: A cohesion problem will surface only in the air fryer, when the batch starts falling apart and it is too late to fix.
steps.calibration: This very test defines "1×" for the flour: the correct amount is the minimum at which the ball passes the test. Always try zero flour first.

steps.title: Shape the balls
steps.what: With damp hands, shape balls of ~30 g each (walnut-sized) and flatten them slightly — they cook more evenly that way. You should get about 20.

equipment.settings: ~30 g per ball; wet your hands with water

steps.done_when: Even, firm balls of uniform size, with no cracks on the surface.
steps.if_skipped: Uneven-sized balls cook unevenly: small ones dry out, large ones stay raw inside.

steps.title: Air fry in the Ninja MAX PRO
steps.what: Spray or brush the balls with oil and arrange them in the basket in a single layer with gaps. Air Fry at ~200 °C for ~12–14 min, turning them at minute 6–7.
steps.done_when: A deep golden, crisp crust on all sides; a broken-open ball is crumbly and cooked through inside, not doughy.
steps.if_skipped: Without turning halfway, the underside stays pale and soft while the top over-dries.
steps.calibration: First-batch calibration is mandatory: at minute 11, break one ball open — if the inside is doughy, add 2 min and check again. Timing shifts with ball size and mixture moisture; after calibration the values become verified for your setup.

notes: All air fryer times and temperatures are estimates (~): they shift with ball size, mixture moisture and the specific machine. Calibrate the first batch per the step 8 instruction — after that, the values become verified for your own conditions.
The amount of flour and the number of pulses are fundamentally not fixed numbers (?): they are determined by the ball test and the consistency test, not by the recipe.
